title: Responses to crizotinib can occur in c-MET overexpressing nonsmall cell lung cancer after developing EGFR-TKI resistance
author: Yanjun Xu; Yun Fan
text:
ABSTRACT
Evidence suggests that activation of the MET signaling pathway might be associated with EGFR-TKI resistance. EGFR TKI-resistant lung cancers often remain sensitive to inhibition of the EGFR pathway; thus, c-MET inhibitors are likely to be effective when combined with continued EGFR-TKI treatment. Here, we described a 56-year-old male who became refractory after first-line gefitinib therapy and was confirmed to have c-MET overexpression without a T790M mutation, c-MET amplification or MET exon 14 alterations. A complete response to crizotinib occurred in this patient. Our case report uncovered the underlying mechanism of c-MET overexpression in affecting EGFR-TKI sensitivity, and crizotinib may assist in overcoming this problem.
Keywords: NSCLC, EGFR, c-MET, crizotinib, resistance, EGFR-TKI, gefitinib
Introduction
Studies have shown that approximately 30–50% of nonsmall cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients in Asia present with somatic mutations in the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) gene in comparison to approximately 10–20% in Caucasians and African Americans.1 Unfortunately, there are approximately 30% of cases of NSCLC that do not experience disease responses to EGFR-TKIs, despite harboring EGFR-mutations.2,3 Most of these patients develop resistance to EGFR-TKIs after an average of approximately 9–14 months.4,5 Approximately 5–20% of secondary resistances are acquired along with MET amplification.6 In contrast, pre-existing resistance in the presence of MET aberrations is rarely detected.7 C-MET is a potentially attractive therapeutic target for overcoming EGFR-TKI resistance.
Some studies have shown that NSCLC with MET amplification or MET ex14 skipping mutations respond to crizotinib treatment.8 However, it is unknown whether lung cancer overexpressing MET might respond to crizotinib and whether MET overexpression and EGFR mutation double-rearranged lung cancer could respond to crizotinib and gefitinib combination treatment.
We herein describe an interesting case of a rapid response to crizotinib in a c-MET overexpressing patient with a pre-existing activating mutation in Ex21 L858R of EGFR. This patient developed drug resistance after first line EGFR-TKI treatment without MET amplification or MET exon 14 alterations but benefited from combination treatment with EGFR-TKI and crizotinib after disease progression.
Case presentation
A 56-year-old Chinese man with a 30 pack-year smoking history presented to our hospital in March 2016, complaining of cough with a right lower lobular lung mass (9.4 x 7 cm). Coarse needle biopsy of the right clavicular lymph node suggested metastatic poorly differentiated carcinoma (adenocarcinoma), IHC: CK5/6(-), ALK(D5F3)(-), ALK-NC(-), ROS1(+, 30%), c-Met(+++, 90%), CK7(+), Napsin A(+), P40(-), P63(-), TTF1(+), Sy(-), and CHG-A\CgA(-) (Figure 1). The molecular detection (ARMS) results showed an EGFR Ex21 L858R mutation. Targeted next-generation sequencing (NGS) of 295 cancer-related genes (Geneseep, China) was performed, revealing an EGFR Ex21 L858R mutation, a BIM heterozygous deletion polymorphism, an RB1 mutation, a TET2 mutation, a DAXX mutation, and an ARID1A mutation. Therefore, the diagnosis of the patient was lung adenocarcinoma with an EGFR Ex21 L858R mutation, staging: cT4N3M0, IIIB.
He received Bevacizumab (500 mg d1, Q3W) plus gefitinib (250 mg po qd) as the first-line treatment and suffered disease progression after 2 months. Digital PCR from the whole blood sample was generated and suggested an Ex21 L858R mutation in the EGFR gene that was Ex20 T790M negative. Then, Bevacizumab plus PCb chemotherapy was applied for two cycles with carboplatin AUC 5, and pemetrexed 500 mg/m2 was given intravenously every 3 weeks. A follow-up CT scan on Jul 7, 2016, revealed disease progression.
At this time, the patient and his family strongly requested palliative surgery, and, after a discussion within the hospital MDT group as well as full communication with the family members, on July 18, 2016, palliative lower right lobe resection +partial middle lobectomy +subclavian lymph node sampling was performed. Three weeks after surgery, CT suggested multiple pulmonary nodules and disease progression.
After reviewing the results of IHC before treatment and after surgery, both results suggested c-Met overexpression (+++, 90%-95%). We further applied FISH for postoperative specimens but found that the MET gene ratio was negative. c-MET amplification was also negative. NGS of the postoperative samples still suggested the presence of an Ex21 L858R mutation in the EGFR, a BIM heterozygous deletion polymorphism, and no c-MET amplification and mutation.
We added crizotinib to his treatment (250 mg po bid) on the basis of applying gefitinib. One month later, the efficacy evaluation was a PR. Since then, the patient has continued to be treated with crizotinib combined with gefitinib. A PET/CT evaluation on 20 Sep 2017 showed a complete response that has been maintained to the present (Figure 2).
To further understand the evolutionary process of the cancer genes in this patient, we put the gene testing results together to draw a schematic diagram of clonal evolution, which is shown in Figure 3. In this case, we performed gene testing at four time points: before treatment (tissue sample, by NGS), after EGFR-TKI exposure (blood sample, by Digital PCR), at the time at surgery (tissue sample, by NGS) and on 28 Aug 2017, when the patient developed a CR (blood sample, by NGS). We observed widespread intratumor heterogeneity in this patient, and 11 subclones were clustered from common and unique mutations of all samples. Subclone-3 was the major subclone, which carried a cancer driver event EGFR L858R mutation.
Discussion
This case requires us to think about the following questions: what are the probable mechanisms among patients with rapid progression of first-generation EGFR TKI resistance?, what are the major activation forms of the MET pathway?, and is it better to apply first-line cotargeted therapy (EGFR TKI+Met pathway inhibition) for patients with both gene changes?
When referring to the first question, we tested for the T790M mutation first after the patient showed resistance to gefitinib, with a negative result. According to the NGS results, the potential mechanism of primary resistance to gefitinib may be due to a BIM heterozygous deletion polymorphism as a partial and co-occurring mutation in RB1, TET2, DAXX, or ARID1A. To determine the impact of co-occurring alterations in promoting tumor progression and response to therapy, Blakely sequenced cell-free DNA (cfDNA) from 1,122 patients with EGFR mutant and 1,008 patients without EGFR-mutant advanced NSCLC. The EGFR-mutant patient cohort had widespread occurrence of additional genetic alterations.9 Thus, intratumor heterogeneity also plays an important role in EGFR-TKIs drug resistance.10 Here, we provided an analysis of cancer gene evolution of this patient, which showed that intratumor heterogeneity and branched subclone evolution play an important role in EGFR-TKI resistance and disease progression. We also observed that disease progression was followed by extensive subclonal diversification.
Abnormal c-MET pathways can arise through mutation, amplification or overexpression. No instances have been reported where MET exon 14-skipping mutations could mediate resistance to EGFR-TKIs. Such mutations have been considered primary oncogenic drivers. In most NSCLC cases, c-MET was not amplified in pretreatment specimens. However, in some instances, patients with EGFR-mutations and primary resistance to EGFR-TKIs had concomitant MET amplification, and such tumors may be inhibited by c-MET inhibitor monotherapy. In our case, the IHC results suggested the overexpression of c-MET protein in tumor tissue, while c-MET amplification and MET ex14-skipping mutations were not detected with FISH and NGS. Interestingly, the patient benefited from treatment with crizotinib. Thus, in the treatment of c-MET-positive lung cancer, we have to consider whether these c-MET variations are most predictive and which are the ideal targets.
MET abnormalities show several patterns, including gene mutations, amplification, protein overexpression and rearrangement, which have all been observed in specific subsets of lung tumors11, but rearrangement is quite rare. Two large randomized controlled phase III trials in previous years12,13 reported that pretreated patients not selected for MET genomic abnormalities who received a MET inhibitor in combination with erlotinib had outcomes approximately the same as those treated with the EGFR-TKI alone. Evidence suggests that patients with high amplification (i.e., MET:CEP7 ratio >5) might have a high response rate (>35%) to MET inhibitors such as crizotinib.14 Paik reported responses to the MET inhibitors crizotinib and cabozantinib in five patients with lung adenocarcinomas bearing the MET ex14 mutation.15 At the 2016 ASCO conference, Yilong Wu reported the efficacy results of a single-arm phase Ib/II study of capmatinib (INC280) +gefitinib in patients with EGFR-mutated, cMET+ (cMET-amplified) NSCLC.16 Their results indicated that capmatinib in combination with gefitinib has efficacy and is well tolerated, particularly among those with high gene copy number (GCN) expression of MET.16 Recently, at the 2017 WCLC meeting, Yilong Wu reported another phase IB trial of savolitinib plus gefitinib for Chinese patients with EGFR-mutant MET-amplified advanced NSCLC and confirmed a partial response was reported in 11 patients (25%).17
At present, the NCCN guideline is recommending the use of crizotinib in the treatment of patients with MET ex14-skipping mutations. However, for MET amplification, the situation is relatively complex, and the best cutoff value for amplification needs to be further determined. Researchers have indicated that the therapeutic efficacy varies with different levels of MET amplification, which is often overlapping with mutations in other driver genes. It is still controversial as to whether MET protein overexpression is a driver gene. The incidence of MET protein overexpression in untreated NSCLC is approximately 33.5% by IHC detection. Although the incidence of MET overexpression in lung adenocarcinoma can be as high as 65%, during the progression of the tumor, it is more often a secondary event driven by other gene activations rather than a driving factor for primary cancer formation or progression.18
However, the overexpression of MET is often associated with resistance to chemo- and radiotherapy.19 Our patient developed resistance to chemotherapy but still benefited from the treatment with crizotinib, which is consistent with other studies. More studies are required to confirm whether c-MET overexpression could be designated as a therapeutic target in MET-positive lung cancers.
When referring to the third question as to whether it is better to apply first-line cotargeted therapy for patients with both gene aberrations, a meta-analysis seems to have answered that question by showing that the addition of a MET inhibitor to an EGFR-TKI has no survival benefit over placebo in patients with NSCLC.20 Seven studies were included in the meta-analysis of a total of 2,577 patients. However, subgroup analysis showed that patients with MET-high NSCLC tended to have longer survival when a MET inhibitor was added (P = 0.06); thus, careful selection of suitable patients to be treated with a combination of MET inhibitors and EGFR-TKI may have positive results. Therefore, early intervention with a combined strategy to prevent the expansion of c-MET aberrant clones may subsequently prevent, rather than overcome, the resistance to EGFR-TKI mediated by c-MET signal aberrations. However, the survival benefit of MET inhibitors remains controversial.
